空军部长公共事务办公室
在空军部着力构建更加互联、更具韧性的“战斗网络”（Battle Network）之际，军方和业界领袖于9月15日在空军与太空军协会“空中、太空与网络大会”的一场专题讨论上，聚焦一个核心难题：如何更快地把作战能力送到作战人员手中。
“下一代战斗管理”专题讨论汇集了柯林斯航空航天公司的Elaine Bitonti、波音公司的退役Maj. Gen. Scott Jobe、SAIC公司的退役Col. Sean Lowe，以及埃尔比特美国公司的退役Maj. Luke Savoie。空军部负责指挥、控制、通信与战斗管理组合采办事务的Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams主持了讨论。
Williams在开场发言中强调，必须超越那些各自独立运行的系统。
Williams说：“空军部不会接受建立在封闭软件栈、黑箱硬件或受限数据接口之上的商业模式。政府必须拥有并管理技术基线，以确保快速迭代升级。”
在Savoie看来，这种开放性必须从体系架构延伸到在作战前沿运行的技术。
“你如何解决边缘的计算部分，从而使这些工具和互联网络在最前沿人员的循环中越来越靠前、越来越快地运行？”萨沃伊（Savoie）问道。
比通蒂（Bitonti）将这一挑战直接与部队中数据的移动联系起来。
“我认为，首先，你知道，从战斗管理角度看，我们明白关键在于我们如何移动数据，”比通蒂说，并解释称，将软件与硬件分离并创建灵活的通信架构，可以让系统在新需求出现时进行适应。
小组成员一致认为，这种灵活性只有在DAF能够快速测试和部署新能力时才有用。
“我认为，对政府而言，关键之一在于快速原型开发、演示，并确保我们拥有行业合作伙伴关系，”乔布（Jobe）说。“为了真正向DAF战斗网络或联合部队证明它，你必须走出去演示它，表明它是真实的。”
乔布指出最近的一个例子：一枚AMRAAM从一架MQ-28 Ghost Bat上发射，并在九个月内与一架E-7 Wedgetail和F/A-18 Hornet完成集成。
“因此，这只是我们所做众多事情中的一个例子，也是快速原型开发和进入实地演示能力的一个例子，”乔布说。
随后，小组转向研发与作战使用之间最大的障碍之一：测试、安全和认证。
洛(Lowe)描述了一个流程：软件会依次经过开发、安全合规、开发测试和作战测试，而每一次转段都可能增加数周或数月的时间。
“这就是为什么会出现数月乃至数年的延误，”洛(Lowe)说。他提到一种做法，即开发测试和作战测试人员与开发人员并肩工作，从而使变更能够更早被发现和解决。“把开发测试与作战测试人员放到合适的位置，尤其是与开发团队在一起，我们就能加快这一进程。”
“ATO流程……其一，它不受项目办公室大多数人的控制，而一旦进入这一环节，确实会让一切戛然而止，”萨沃伊(Savoie)说，并呼吁对网络安全、信息技术安全和认证流程进行更广泛的审视。
乔布(Jobe)同样指出，安全环境是一个政策和决策可以更快推进的领域。
“我认为我们很可能可以快得多，”乔布说。“也许对采办系统内的人员进行一些沟通和教育可能会有所裨益。”
对比通蒂(Bitonti)而言，各军种与联盟伙伴之间的数据共享构成了另一项政策挑战。
“我们谈到非常希望作为联合部队行动，也与我们的联盟伙伴共同行动，但在关于我们可以和不能共享哪些数据的规则集方面，存在多重限制，也就是政策限制，”她说。
“目前，造成我们在共享数据方面一些困难的，实际上并不是技术障碍。而是政策障碍。”
在专题讨论结束时，Williams 把讨论拉回到空军部（DAF）的职责上，即以不断演变的作战所要求的速度交付能力。
“采办是一项作战职能，”Williams 说。“我们必须以作战相关性所需的速度，交付开放、有韧性、软件驱动的能力。”

items.title: Never Underestimate the Houthis
items.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels are in a position to shape the next phase of the conflict between the United States and Iran if they attempt to renew their blockade of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. And no one should assume that a deal with Iran will bind what the Houthis do next.
items.body:
Just a few years ago, Yemen's Houthi rebels were second- or third-tier members of Iran's “Axis of Resistance,” prompting policymakers to treat them as a subsidiary of Tehran. But while they benefit from Iranian weapons, training and know-how, the Houthis also have their own interests at heart—and behave accordingly.

This armed group that controls much of northern Yemen is in position to shape the next phase of the conflict between the United States and Iran if they attempt to renew their blockade of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The Houthis could reignite the war in Yemen, scuttle efforts to make a deal with Iran and draw the United States even deeper into the region's conflicts.

A key assumption going into the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, which began in February, was that Iran's proxy militias had been critically weakened. Hezbollah, the militant group in Lebanon that was once Iran's most powerful partner in the region, suffered heavy blows from Israel during the Gaza war, as did Hamas. Iran lost another key ally when Bashar al-Assad's regime in Syria collapsed in December 2024.

The Houthis, whose military capacity had also been weakened by U.S. strikes in 2024–25, did not jump back into the fray right away when the United States and Israel began striking Iran this year, seemingly sparing them similar blows.

Perhaps they were biding their time. Because of a quirk of geography, the Houthis are able to disrupt commercial traffic in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a choke point at the entry to the Red Sea, through which 12 percent to 15 percent of maritime trade travels. At the other end of the Red Sea lies the Suez Canal, a vital route for oil and liquefied natural gas headed to North American and European markets. With Iran effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis are now in an unusually powerful position.

With Iran effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis are now in an unusually powerful position.

They have come far in global influence since seizing Yemen's capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and expelling the internationally recognized government from the city in early 2015. When the rebel forces pushed south in March of that year, in an attempt to take over territory in southern Yemen, a coalition led by Saudi Arabia and backed by the United States intervened.

The once localized war became a regional conflict and a devastating humanitarian crisis. Finally, facing a stalemate and significant international pressure, both sides agreed to a U.N.-brokered cease-fire in April 2022. By that point, the Houthis had created a de facto state in northern Yemen, while the weak Saudi-backed government nominally ruled parts of the south and west.

The Houthis flexed their muscles by attacking shipping vessels in the Red Sea early in the Israel-Gaza war that started in 2023. Using low-cost, low-tech equipment like one-way attack drones, missiles and unmanned surface vessels, the Houthis made the crossing more dangerous, driving up the cost of insuring commercial ships as much as twentyfold, effectively closing the strait. The only alternate route forced ships around the southern tip of the African continent, an extra 4,000 or more nautical miles, increasing shipping costs.

Last month, the Houthis resumed attacks on Red Sea shipping, striking Saudi-linked commercial oil tankers and hitting Saudi energy and transportation infrastructure. They were responding to what they claimed were Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa Airport's runway on July 13, seemingly in an effort to prevent an incoming Iranian flight from landing. For now, commercial ships continue to transit the Red Sea, although tanker traffic has declined substantially over the past month. Houthi attacks have also continued on ships the group claims are Saudi-aligned, and an attack on a cargo ship on Aug. 12 included the first reported fatalities of this latest round of attacks.

In recent days, the Houthis have claimed attacks on a ship in the Red Sea port of Mokha, which is held by forces allied with the internationally recognized government of Yemen, and on airports and oil refinery infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

With the effective closure of Hormuz, the Red Sea-Suez route has become even more important. Most notably, Saudi Arabia had sought to avoid Hormuz by routing crude oil via a pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu on its western coast. The new Houthi attacks have disrupted that option. The near closure of both Hormuz and the Suez routes could compound problems for global trade, pushing the cost of oil and inflation even higher.

Now the Houthis are positioned to step up their involvement in an already raging regional conflagration, complicating efforts to end it. Some may assume that this move is at the behest of Iran, but the reality is likely more complicated.

Highly attuned to their own interests and pragmatic in the international arena, the Houthis have proved savvy at choosing when to enter or escalate conflicts. When they attacked shipping in the Red Sea in 2023–25, for example, they said it was to pressure Israel to de-escalate its operations in Gaza. The strikes also bolstered their legitimacy in the territory they control in northern Yemen, diverting attention from their governance failures at a time when their popularity had eroded.

The Houthis have proved savvy at choosing when to enter or escalate conflicts.

This time, the Houthis appear to see an opening to gain leverage in negotiations with Saudi Arabia to reach a political settlement in the Yemeni war—or an opportunity to resume attacks against the internationally backed government.

The previous round of Houthi attacks, in 2023–25, had a significant but ultimately manageable effect on the global economy. Estimates suggested that the ensuing shipping disruptions would have a small impact on inflation. The economic effects of closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the same time as Hormuz are likely to be more dire.

While the United States looks to wind down the war with Iran, the Houthis are threatening to resume their war in Yemen, which would likely draw in Saudi Arabia, menace the global oil trade and keep the region unstable.

It will be difficult to de-escalate regional tensions without addressing the Houthis' threat directly, rather than assuming it can be resolved by dealing with their supposed boss, Iran. At the same time, no one should assume that a deal with Iran will bind what the Houthis do next. The international community should confront them as a pragmatic and dangerous actor making decisions in their own self-interest.
items.zhFull:
就在几年前，也门胡塞叛军还只是伊朗“抵抗轴心”中的二线或三线成员，这促使政策制定者将其视为德黑兰的附属。然而，尽管他们受益于伊朗的武器、训练和技术，胡塞武装也有自己的利益考量，并据此行事。

这支控制也门北部大片地区的武装组织，如果试图重启对曼德海峡的封锁，就有能力影响美国与伊朗冲突的下一阶段。胡塞武装可能重新点燃也门战争，破坏与伊朗达成协议的努力，并把美国进一步拖入该地区的冲突。

在2月开始的美以对伊朗袭击中，一个关键假设是伊朗的代理民兵已遭到严重削弱。黎巴嫩激进组织真主党曾是伊朗在该地区最强大的伙伴，在加沙战争期间遭到以色列重创，哈马斯也是如此。2024年12月，叙利亚巴沙尔·阿萨德 (Bashar al-Assad) 政权垮台，伊朗又失去一个关键盟友。

胡塞武装的军事能力也曾因美国在2024—25年的打击而遭到削弱；当美国和以色列今年开始打击伊朗时，他们并未立即重新加入战团，似乎因此免遭类似打击。

也许他们是在等待时机。由于地理上的特殊条件，胡塞武装能够扰乱曼德海峡的商业航运；这条海峡是红海入口处的咽喉要道，12%至15%的海上贸易经此通行。红海另一端是苏伊士运河，这是石油和液化天然气运往北美和欧洲市场的重要通道。随着伊朗实际上封锁霍尔木兹海峡，胡塞武装如今处于异常强大的地位。

随着伊朗实际上封锁霍尔木兹海峡，胡塞武装如今处于异常强大的地位。

自2014年夺取也门首都萨那，并于2015年初将国际公认的政府赶出该市以来，他们在全球影响力方面已取得长足进展。当年3月，叛军向南推进，试图夺取也门南部领土，沙特阿拉伯领导、美国支持的联军随即介入。

这场一度局部化的战争演变为地区冲突和毁灭性的人道主义危机。最终，面对僵局和巨大的国际压力，双方于2022年4月同意接受联合国斡旋的停火。到那时，胡塞武装已在也门北部建立了一个事实上的国家，而沙特支持的软弱政府名义上统治着南部和西部的部分地区。

胡塞武装在2023年爆发的以色列-加沙战争初期通过袭击红海航运船只来展示实力。他们使用单向攻击无人机、导弹和无人水面艇等低成本、低技术装备，使这一航道穿越变得更加危险，将商船保险费率推高至原来的二十倍之多，实际上封锁了该海峡。唯一的替代航线迫使船只绕行非洲大陆南端，额外航行4,000 nautical miles以上，推高了航运成本。

上个月，胡塞武装恢复对红海航运的袭击，打击与沙特有关联的商用油轮，并袭击沙特的能源和交通基础设施。他们称此举是对沙特7月13日空袭萨那机场跑道的回应，后者似乎意在阻止一架即将抵达的伊朗航班降落。目前，商船仍在继续穿行红海，尽管过去一个月油轮运输量大幅下降。胡塞武装还继续袭击其声称与沙特结盟的船只，而8月12日对一艘货船的袭击中出现了本轮袭击中首批报告的死亡事件。

近日，胡塞武装声称袭击了红海摩卡港的一艘船只——该港由与也门国际公认政府结盟的武装力量控制——以及沙特阿拉伯的机场和炼油厂基础设施。

随着霍尔木兹海峡实际关闭，红海—苏伊士航线变得更加重要。最突出的是，沙特阿拉伯曾试图通过管道将原油输送至其西海岸的延布港，以避开霍尔木兹海峡。胡塞武装的新一轮袭击使这一选择受阻。霍尔木兹海峡和红海—苏伊士航线近乎同时关闭，可能使全球贸易问题雪上加霜，进一步推高油价和通胀。

如今，胡塞武装已有条件加大介入这场本已熊熊燃烧的地区冲突，使结束冲突的努力更加复杂。一些人可能认为此举是应伊朗指使，但实际情况可能更为复杂。

胡塞武装高度关注自身利益，在国际舞台上行事务实，在何时介入或升级冲突的问题上表现出精明的判断力。例如，在2023—2025年袭击红海航运时，他们称此举是为了向以色列施压，促使其缓和在加沙的军事行动。这些袭击还增强了其在也门北部所控制地区的合法性，在其支持率下滑之际转移了人们对其治理失败的注意力。

胡塞武装在何时介入或升级冲突的问题上表现得相当精明。

这一次，胡塞武装似乎看到了在与沙特阿拉伯谈判中获取筹码、推动也门战争政治解决的机会——或者是恢复对国际社会支持的政府发动袭击的契机。

上一轮胡塞武装袭击（2023—2025年）对全球经济造成了显著但最终尚可消化的影响。当时的评估认为，随之而来的航运中断对通胀的影响有限。而一旦曼德海峡与霍尔木兹海峡同时被封锁，其经济后果可能更为严峻。

在美国寻求结束与伊朗的战争之际，胡塞武装却威胁要在也门重启战事，这很可能把沙特阿拉伯卷入其中，威胁全球石油贸易，并使该地区持续动荡不安。

如果不直接应对胡塞武装的威胁，而是想当然地认为通过与其所谓的后台伊朗打交道就能解决问题，那么缓和地区紧张局势将十分困难。与此同时，任何人都不应以为与伊朗达成协议就能约束胡塞武装接下来的行动。国际社会应当把他们视为一个务实而危险、依据自身利益行事的行动方来加以应对。

随着霍尔木兹海峡实际关闭，红海—苏伊士航线变得更加重要。最突出的是，沙特阿拉伯曾试图通过管道将原油输送至其西海岸的延布港，以避开霍尔木兹海峡。胡塞武装的新一轮袭击使这一选择受阻。霍尔木兹海峡和红海—苏伊士航线近乎同时关闭，可能使全球贸易问题雪上加霜，进一步推高油价和通胀。
如今，胡塞武装已有条件加大介入这场本已熊熊燃烧的地区冲突，使结束冲突的努力更加复杂。一些人可能认为此举是应伊朗指使，但实际情况可能更为复杂。
胡塞武装高度关注自身利益，在国际舞台上行事务实，在何时介入或升级冲突的问题上表现出精明的判断力。例如，在2023—2025年袭击红海航运时，他们称此举是为了向以色列施压，促使其缓和在加沙的军事行动。这些袭击还增强了其在也门北部所控制地区的合法性，在其支持率下滑之际转移了人们对其治理失败的注意力。
胡塞武装在何时介入或升级冲突的问题上表现得相当精明。
这一次，胡塞武装似乎看到了在与沙特阿拉伯谈判中获取筹码、推动也门战争政治解决的机会——或者是恢复对国际社会支持的政府发动袭击的契机。
上一轮胡塞武装袭击（2023—2025年）对全球经济造成了显著但最终尚可消化的影响。当时的评估认为，随之而来的航运中断对通胀的影响有限。而一旦曼德海峡与霍尔木兹海峡同时被封锁，其经济后果可能更为严峻。
在美国寻求结束与伊朗的战争之际，胡塞武装却威胁要在也门重启战事，这很可能把沙特阿拉伯卷入其中，威胁全球石油贸易，并使该地区持续动荡不安。
如果不直接应对胡塞武装的威胁，而是想当然地认为通过与其所谓的后台伊朗打交道就能解决问题，那么缓和地区紧张局势将十分困难。与此同时，任何人都不应以为与伊朗达成协议就能约束胡塞武装接下来的行动。国际社会应当把他们视为一个务实而危险、依据自身利益行事的行动方来加以应对。

items.title: Mind over miles: Mental grit propels champions at 2026 Air Force Marathon
items.author: Megan Purves
items.summary: More than 9,000 runners participated in the 30th annual Air Force Marathon at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, showcasing physical stamina and mental toughness.
items.body:
Published Sept. 19, 2026

By Megan Purves

88th Air Base Wing Public Affairs

Every mile of a race is a physical negotiation — a stark reminder that while the human body has limits, the mind can be trained to push past them.

Leading the charge were full marathon champions U.S. Space Force 1st Lt. Nicholas McKenzie, Vandenberg Space Force Base , California with a time of 2:34:31 and Kayla Rice, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base employee, with a time of 2:56:39.

However, for McKenzie, the mental turning point came during the race’s most solemn stretch.

“Around mile 21, it definitely starts to get hard. But running and seeing the tributes to our fallen service members was emotional and heartwarming. It really helped me stay motivated to get to the end. Seeing that helps you realize the ultimate sacrifice they gave, and it motivated me to dig a little deeper.”

For Rice, crossing the finish line as the women’s champion marked the culmination of years of dedicated training right on her home base at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.

“I feel incredible. This has been a goal I’ve been working toward for the past few years, and it’s great to finally achieve it,” Rice said. “This is my fourth time running it, so every year it’s been my goal to just get a little bit faster and eventually get where I am today. It was a big personal record for me, and getting to see all my friends, family, coworkers, and teammates out on the course was amazing.”

Sharing that spotlight of sheer determination were half-marathon champions Simon Heys, a civilian runner at 1:05:45 and 2nd Lt. Allyson Peterson, Ramstein Air Base , with a time of 1:19:10.

For Heys, pushing through the half-marathon course was a personal way to show gratitude for military service members.

“It was special,” Heys said. “I really wanted to come here and just run as hard as I could. I wanted to put the grind out there, like the men and women who fight for this country do every day.”

Peterson, competing in her first half marathon, relied on strategic pacing and late-race momentum to secure her victory.

“I’ve been looking forward to this race,” she said. “I had a great group of guys to chase coming down for the last like six miles. So, I was just focusing on closing that gap.”

Beyond individual determination on the course, Department of the Air Force leadership underscored how physical discipline and community support directly reinforce the strength and readiness of the joint force.

“If I have one message for you today, thank you for showing up to do hard things,” said Matthew L. Lohmeier , 29th Under Secretary of the Air Force. “Thank you for working together as a community, both to support the 30th Air Force Marathon and to make the Department of the Air Force and the entire joint force a better place to work, a more lethal, ready force. And thank you for taking care of yourselves to be a part of our ready force.”

As the cheers from the finish line festival filled the air and the champions took their places at the awards ceremony, the legacy of the 2026 race extended beyond the trophy stands. For the thousands who crossed the finish line, the race was more than an athletic showcase. It was a masterclass in mental readiness, proving that when the mission demands endurance, disciplined preparation will always carry us through.

Here’s a look at the top three men’s and women’s finishers in the full marathon and half marathon:

*Unofficial times according to RacePenguin, the Air Force Marathon’s race tracker*

MEN’S FULL MARATHON 1st: — Nick McKenzie 2 hours, 34 minutes, 31 seconds 2nd: — Hunter Boyer 2:40:01 3rd: — Jack Walker 2:41:24

WOMEN’S FULL MARATHON 1st: — Kayla Rice 2:56:39 2nd: — Lindsay Babish 3:09:12 3rd: — Kristen Petrosky 3:14:06

MEN’S HALF-MARATHON 1st: — Simon Heys 1:05:45 2nd: — Peter Allegre 1:11:01 3rd: — Patrick Konecny 1:11:13

WOMEN’S HALF-MARATHON 1st: — Allyson Peterson 1:19:10 2nd: — Kelsi Harris 1:24:52 3rd: — Corinne Yorkman 1:26:26

To see more race results including 10K, 5K, wheeled hand-crank full marathon, wheeled push-rim full marathon, visit www.usafmarathon.com .

More imagery will be available in the coming days at https://www.dvidshub.net/unit/88ABW .

I’m ecstatic – it’s a great day with super energy out on the course and beautiful weather. This is my second time running the Air Force Marathon, and I’m super grateful for all the volunteers, the support, and all the other runners out here getting it done today.

It was a big personal record for me, and getting to see all my friends, family, coworkers, and teammates out on the course was amazing.

Thank you for working together as a community, both to support the 30th Air Force Marathon and to make the Department of the Air Force and the entire joint force a better place to work, a more lethal, ready force. And thank you for taking care of yourselves to be a part of our ready force.

items.title: A Design Lab Pilot to Inform Strategies for Expanding Access to Medications for Opioid Use Disorder in Community Mental Health Centers
items.author: Bradley D. Stein
items.summary: A pilot Design Lab identified barriers and strategies to improving access to medications for opioid use disorder in community mental health settings. Expanding insurer reimbursement via a learning exchange was seen as most impactful and feasible.
items.body:
ResearchPublished Sep 18, 2026

This pilot Design Lab engaged clients, clinic leaders, and policy experts to identify barriers and strategies for expanding access to medications for opioid use disorder. Stigma, workforce shortages, regulatory complexity, and payment limitations emerged as key challenges. Expanding insurer reimbursement through a structured learning exchange was rated highest in impact and feasibility, suggesting cross-sector collaboration may advance access.

items.title: COMAMC emphasizes air mobility’s role in ‘Flying and Fixing to Fight and Win’ at AFA 2026
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, commander of Air Mobility Command, joined fellow commanders and senior leaders to address service members, defense industry partners and journalists during the 2026 AFA Air, Space and Cyber Conference.
items.body:
Published Sept. 17, 2026

Air Mobility Command Public Affairs

Tulley joined Gen. S. L. Davis , commander of Air Force Global Strike Command , Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry , commander of Air Force Materiel Command and Maj. Gen. Jon Eberlan , Director of Logistics, Engineering and Force Protection, Headquarters Air Combat Command , for a panel discussion focused on the Chief of Staff of the Air Force 's operational imperative to fly and fix aircraft to deter adversaries and, if deterrence fails, to fight and win decisively in contested theaters.

Addressing the current tempo of operations, Tulley highlighted that Air Mobility Command has roughly 300 aircraft deployed across several geographic combatant commands, supported by approximately 10,000 Airmen operating at an intense tempo. He stressed that strategic air refueling is only a fraction of the total support required to sustain the Joint Force. AMC also delivers the supplies, the munitions, the sustainment and the base operating support that combatant commanders count on.

"Air refueling is just part of the story," Tulley said. "What strikes me is the lessons that they're bringing back. We've got a generation of Airmen who are going to come back home with combat experience that will be priceless for [countering] our pacing threat."

When asked about managing readiness with a largely fixed inventory of aircraft, Tulley challenged legacy, binary models of preparedness, advocating for systems that measure combat capability in a protracted fight.

"When we think about readiness in Air Mobility Command, we really think about answering four questions: readiness of what, for what, for when, and at what cost. But when we look at the lessons in Ukraine, we also have to ask ourselves: for how long?" Tulley stated. "Readiness in contact is the way we're approaching this."

To illustrate the joint teamwork required to generate readiness in contact, Tulley noted that AFMC pushed forward depot-level capabilities to Royal Air Force Mildenhall, United Kingdom, where maintenance teams have successfully swapped 30 KC-135 Stratotanker boom assemblies in-theater rather than flying the aircraft back to the United States for repairs.

Turning to the challenges of concurrent global demand and operating across multiple theaters, Tulley explained that AMC functions as the global air component to U.S. Transportation Command , balancing requirements across 11 combatant commands.

Addressing the pilot pipeline and training constraints, Tulley emphasized that the command is looking at the entire enterprise to ensure experienced aircrews are in operational squadrons.

"At the end of the day, we really need experience in the squadrons," Tulley said, noting that he recently convened a team to examine how the command can simplify its training requirements. "How much time do we spend in training now? What are our requirements for all of our mission sets. How can we simplify that? Always assure we have the basic level of readiness to keep the global transportation system operating, but then tailor the training we need for that high-end fight."

To highlight the reality of operating and fixing aircraft while under fire, Tulley recounted a recent real-world mission where a KC-135 aircrew and maintenance team sheltered during a ballistic missile attack, then immediately emerged to contain a major fuel leak, patch shrapnel holes and repair the aircraft so it could complete a transoceanic flight home for depot restoration. Tulley stressed that readiness is a vital, continuous process for the command.

"Pretty simple for us: train like you fight, train like you will fight in a peer fight," Tulley said. "Training like you fight has got to stress our Airmen. It’s got to train them to be ready for those stresses, and then do it again and again and again."

Tulley concluded by discussing the evolution of contested logistics, highlighting that AMC has adapted to track detailed replacement parts for aircraft in contested theaters, alongside combat munitions shipments.

"One of the things I'd say about logistics and supply lines are that we are good, but we're getting better," Tulley stated. "If you can get to the granularity and the precision to say, 'Okay, I need these [Mission Impaired Capability Awaiting Parts] delivered with those munitions,' you're increasing combat capability. You're turning aircraft back into the fight faster."

As AMC continues to operate at a sustained global tempo, Tulley emphasized that the command’s advantage rests on its ability to generate, sustain and regenerate combat capability under contested conditions. By integrating maintenance, logistics, training and operational planning across the mobility enterprise, AMC is working to ensure its Airmen and aircraft can support the Joint Force wherever and whenever they are needed.

items.title: Preserving Jobs and Tax Revenue in the Age of AI: Q&A with Carter Price
items.summary: Carter Price, a mathematician at RAND and co-director of the RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative, discusses ways to rebalance the tax code so that it doesn't incentivize employers to replace humans with AI.
items.body:
If AI starts to replace jobs, it isn't just American workers who will feel the loss of income. So will the U.S. Treasury.

Nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue comes from taxes levied on human labor, a recent RAND study noted. That revenue will not be easy to make up if AI starts to put large numbers of people out of work.

Carter Price has been looking for ways to rebalance the tax code so that it doesn't incentivize employers to replace humans with AI. He's a mathematician at RAND and co-director of the RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative. And he has an idea for how to give workers an edge in the age of AI.

How does the existing tax code disincentivize keeping human workers on the job?

We went through all 7,000 pages of the tax code with a tool we built as part of the RAND Budget Model Initiative. It allows us to identify every provision, every line item, and its implications. There's a lot in there. But we identified several places where the existing U.S tax code works against companies hiring or keeping workers.

The employer payroll tax is one obvious example. Companies have to pay that tax for every worker they hire, so more workers means more expense. Meanwhile, the tax code allows companies to write off the depreciation of big, expensive assets early, before those assets actually wear out. That can make buying something like a robotic system much more cost-effective—which makes that tax write-off a direct subsidy for displacing human workers.

What's your idea to change the incentives here?

You and I pay progressive taxes on our income. That means if we make more money, we move into a higher tax bracket.

Our idea is somewhat similar, but for companies. The government would tax high corporate profits per worker in addition to taxing their income overall.

Imagine a company makes $1 million in profit and has 100 employees. Its profit per worker is $10,000. Now let's say that company brings in a lot of AI and lays off all but ten of its workers. Now its profit per worker is $100,000, and it just moved into a higher tax bracket. It's going to pay more in taxes for that same $1 million in profit.

AI might still be so much more efficient that it still makes sense for some companies to replace those workers. This tax structure wouldn't stand in the way of that.

But where the current tax code sometimes disincentivizes keeping human workers, our proposed change would flip the script. It would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What else did your tax code analysis find that could help promote employment?

We found a lot of special, niche provisions that are just scattered throughout the tax code. You could eliminate those and really clean everything up. There are three different clean-energy vehicle tax provisions, for example, and they all do pretty much the same thing.

These niche provisions pointed us to a suite of changes that could really make a difference. The government could eliminate those special tax breaks. That would bring in additional revenue.

The federal government could then eliminate the employer payroll tax and replace it with two business taxes: one a flat tax on business revenue, and the other the per-worker tax on high profits.

Companies would be no worse off. The government would balance the loss of revenue from eliminating the payroll tax with an increase from eliminating special tax carve-outs. And we'd be incentivizing human employment instead of using tax breaks to incentivize things like investments in distilled spirits.

Our proposed change would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What would it take to implement those changes?

It takes an act of Congress to change the Internal Revenue Code. But that's a low barrier compared to what some other popular policy ideas that are floating around would face. For example, a value-added tax, which would be like a nationwide sales tax, would require an entirely new tax-collection infrastructure. And a federal wealth tax, which could generate revenue from huge concentrations of wealth, would require a constitutional amendment in addition to new tax-collection infrastructure.

By contrast, policymakers could at least theoretically wake up tomorrow and pass a law that would make the tax code more robust by reducing its dependence on income from labor.

Furthermore, simplifying the tax code would give people back millions of hours that they currently spend filling out forms. It would improve the efficiency of the economy, and that's something everyone can like.

What motivates you to do this work?

I'm a mathematician. And there have been a lot of headlines about the advances that AI models have made in mathematics in particular. AI can generate code that would take a human hours, or even days, to write. I'm biased, but I think human mathematicians still provide a lot of value that AI can't fully replace. I'm not sure that will be true forever. But until that changes, we shouldn't rush into replacing workers with AI, and our tax code certainly shouldn't incentivize employers to do so.

items.title: DAF Battle Network driving multi-domain integration, decision advantage
items.author: Morgan Brown
items.summary: Panelists detailed how open-architecture standards, joint cross-domain data integration, and collaborative acquisition models provide warfighters with real-time decision advantage.
items.body:
Published Sept. 16, 2026

By Morgan Brown

DAF PAE C3BM Public Affairs

Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams , Dr. Bryan Tipton and Col. Raj Agrawal delivered a clear message on the “DAF Battle Network: Why is it crucial?” panel during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Sept. 15. The panel, moderated by Heather Penney, director of studies and research at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, traced how the DAF Battle Network has transitioned from a conceptual architecture into a real-time operational capability that commanders, operators, and joint warfighters are actively employing today. “The DAF Battle Network is not about a single platform or program,” said Williams, the Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Command, Control, Communications and Battle Management . “It is about connecting the capabilities the department already has, bringing in the capabilities it needs next, and making sure they work together to give warfighters resilient decision advantage.”

This operational reality was reinforced by lessons from recent operations. Tipton, chief of architecture and systems engineering for C3BM, noted the real-world impact the DAF Battle Network has already enabled, including hybrid architecture, edge computing, air operations center upgrades, and deploying the Tactical Operations Center-Light prototype. He also highlighted integrating with the Joint Fires Network and the Navy to put JFN into test and operational use, bringing new capabilities such as artificial intelligence into AOCs, and enabling dynamic mission planning.

“We’re also overhauling beyond-line-of-sight and line-of-sight communications,” Tipton continued. “Ground and air capabilities are now connecting to the Space Force’s Space Data Network . Looking forward, a good DAF Battle Network is one where integration becomes easy.”

He said major emerging efforts are also ongoing with point defense and AI.

“The future is now, and it’s real,” he said. To deliver the network, Williams detailed how his role as the DAF Battle Network's integrating PAE differs from standard platform acquisition. Under the mission-focused PAE model launched in January 2026, he wields DAF-level acquisition authority, allowing his office to enforce open-architecture standards and certify interoperability across its roughly 50 core programs of record, and beyond. “It takes extreme teamwork with our PAE and other PAEs across the Air Force,” Williams said. “And it takes Dr. Tipton’s team building the foundation that is the DAF Battle Network in order to truly integrate to scale ahead of the threat.”

Tipton emphasized that maintaining a robust, multilayered transport network is what allows the joint force to move data under intense adversary electronic warfare threats. This data-transport capability is what completes long-range kill chains at the speed of relevance.

“The DAF Battle Network is designed as a system of systems, not as a single-domain solution,” Tipton said. “Different layers provide different operational value, and the strength of the architecture comes from integration across those layers.” Addressing how the operational network bridges domains, Agrawal, the military deputy for space for C3BM, explained that orbital assets like the Space Data Network and space-based moving target indicators are designed to sync in real time with atmospheric platforms. Rather than one domain replacing another, the operational advantage comes from the redundancy and multiple tactical options that this integrated system of systems provides to commanders. “Operators and acquirers are both warfighters,” Agrawal said. “If an operator isn’t inviting acquirers into joint planning sessions, or if an acquirer isn’t engaging operators, they are missing the mark. Our senior leaders have made it possible for us to work together; now it’s time for the joint force to execute as one unified team.”

Ultimately, the panel concluded that the true measure of the DAF Battle Network's success is not a future roadmap or the volume of systems fielded. Instead, success is defined by the operational options it delivers to the warfighter today, giving commanders the decision-making advantage to outpace and outmaneuver adversaries in dynamic, contested environments.

items.title: AMC deputy commander emphasizes long-range airpower, mobility integration at AFA 2026
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: AMC's deputy commander joined military and defense industry leaders to address service members, partners and journalists on the evolving demands of long-range airpower during the 2026 AFA Air, Space and Cyber Conference.
items.body:
Published Sept. 16, 2026

Air Mobility Command Public Affairs

Donohue joined Maj. Gen. Ty W. Neuman , commander of Eighth Air Force and the Joint-Global Strike Operations Center, and Jamie Burgess, vice president and general manager of Mobility, Surveillance and Bombers at Boeing, for a panel discussing long-range airpower with a focus on Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.

During the discussion, Donohue highlighted the essential role of tanker and strategic airlift platforms in bridging global distances to generate decisive combat power without requiring forward-prepositioned strike forces, emphasizing the historic performance of mobility Airmen who did not miss a single Air Refueling Control Time during recent high-tempo operations.

“When we think about the way we've been able to project power, whether it be from the continental United States or from other locations where it's forward-postured, Air Mobility Command, the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve Command — who are undergoing the biggest mobilization in a generation or two — have been committed all in and extraordinarily effective,” Donohue said. “A tanker fleet that is largely defined by 70-year-old aircraft, sustained by extraordinary maintainers and supported by a global enroute structure to ensure it is ready to meet the challenge, has delivered.”

Echoing the strategic synergy required for global strike, Neuman emphasized that bombers and tankers operate as an inseparable system of systems when executing deep-penetration strikes.

“In the near term, we have to have a combat bomber force that has the long-range strike capability, supported by our AMC brethren, to get to the fight with the appropriate capabilities to inflict the necessary pain and suffering on the adversary,” Neuman said.

“Largely today, some of our forces still operate the way they did 20 years ago, and they don’t have the connectivity that you have when you get on your flights to head home,” Donohue explained. “Epic Fury and Midnight Hammer underscored the importance that connectivity plays — not only to our own survivability, but more importantly, to the success of the Joint Force.”

To illustrate the scale of joint warfighting interoperability, Donohue highlighted the massive refueling and airlift footprint required to launch and recover global strike packages.

“When we talk about Midnight Hammer, most public attention rightly focuses on the extraordinary stealth bomber aircrews who executed the mission. What most Americans don’t fully understand is the dozens and dozens of tankers and airlift assets that were necessary to make that happen,” Donohue stated.

Looking ahead, Donohue cautioned that while the acquisition of the KC-46A Pegasus continues to deliver critical capability, the Air Force must remain clear-eyed about the timelines required to modernize the mobility enterprise.

“The last KC-135 pilot has not been born,” Donohue said. “That is just a statement of fact when we consider the time it takes to modernize and so we will have to sustain our legacy platform as well as our newest platforms and ensure that the Joint Force is supported by being able to execute the mission.”

Donohue concluded by expressing his deep gratitude for the Airmen across active, Guard and Reserve components who make global reach a reality every day.

“The nation should be proud of its mobility Airmen,” Donohue concluded. “Whether it’s in our global AOC, the 618th Air Operations Center, our contingency response, or our global air mobility support structure…we have set the theater. And then ultimately, to the tanker aircrews who made every one of the [Air Refueling Control Times] to ensure that [Neuman’s] team can deliver the desired effects, we should all be proud of what that force is able to accomplish.”

items.title: Air Force leaders chart path to future fight
items.author: Senior Airman Malia Heemsoth
items.summary: Air Force senior leaders at the 2026 Air, Space and Cyber Conference discussed adapting to contested environments while balancing current readiness with future modernization.
items.body:
Published Sept. 16, 2026

By Senior Airman Malia Heemsoth

Secretary of the Air Force Public Affairs

Air Force senior leaders discussed how the service can adapt to a contested environment, balance current readiness with future modernization and turn emerging capabilities into combat power during a panel at the Air and Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space and Cyber Conference Sept. 14. The panel featured Gen. Kevin Schneider , commander, Pacific Air Forces; Gen. Adrian L. Spain , commander, Air Combat Command; Lt. Gen. Kenyon Bell , deputy chief of staff for Logistics, Engineering and Force Protection; and Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi , Air Force chief modernization officer. The conversation began with lessons from recent operations and how those experiences are shaping the future force. Schneider identified command and control, agile combat employment and resiliency as key areas for the Air Force moving forward, emphasizing the need for stronger command and control nodes, resilient data pathways and logistics capable of operating under pressure. Spain reinforced the changing nature of the operating environment, pointing to the vulnerability of bases and the need to generate combat airpower while under attack. “We do not operate from sanctuary any longer,” Spain emphasized. “Our bases are under attack, and we have to continue to generate air power in spite of that.” That reality also changes how the service approaches logistics and force protection. Bell stressed that preparing for the future fight means preparing Airmen and infrastructure for conditions they cannot always predict. “The era of uncontested logistics is over,” Bell said, highlighting the need to sustain and regenerate forces while operating in contested environments. For Niemi, recent operations also reinforced the need to accelerate investments in point defense, a rapidly expanding mission designed to safeguard air bases against a full spectrum of airborne threats, and rethink the balance between a small number of highly capable platforms and a broader force able to generate mass. The modernization challenge, however, is not simply determining what the Air Force needs next. Leaders must also decide how much risk the service can accept today to build that future force. Schneider explained that each level of the Air Force operates on a different timeline, with operational commanders closest to the immediate risk. “The operational end user, whoever has OPCON, TACON, owns the risk to mission and the risk to force to the Joint Force commander,” Schneider said. His role, he added, is to communicate that warfighter risk throughout the service so leaders can make informed decisions about the transition from current readiness to future modernization. Spain described how ACC is balancing the immediate demands of presenting forces to combatant commanders with requirements extending decades into the future. While the force fighting within the next five years may look similar to today's force, he noted that it could look different a decade plus from now. Niemi emphasized just how far ahead modernization decisions must look to deliver effective operational capabilities for tomorrow’s Airmen. “We're trying to make a decision now and anticipate what the world is going to look like in 2033,” Niemi explained, noting that decisions made today may not deliver capabilities for years. The tension in meeting today’s operational needs while shaping tomorrow’s force is an important part of the process rather than a problem to eliminate, Spain discussed. “A healthy process here is always under tension,” Spain said. “It shouldn't be that we all agree all the time or we wouldn’t be giving the Chief and SecAF the info they need to make fully informed decisions.” The panel then turned to how the Air Force can move emerging capabilities from development into the hands of the warfighter. Niemi said the service should avoid trying to solve every problem at the headquarters level and instead allow operational commanders to experiment with new tools and determine what works. “What I'm trying to focus on is to get it close enough that when it goes down to Gen. Spain or Gen. Schneider, that they have enough to be able to figure out what right actually looks like when I give them an 80% solution,” Niemi said. Schneider similarly said that modernization cannot stop at acquiring a new platform, but must also include the sustainment of the program. “It's more than just the equipment or the shiny thing that sits on a ramp,” Schneider said. “It's everything that enables it or allows it to be successful.” Spain highlighted the difficulty of introducing new capabilities into established communities. New capabilities, he explained, require commanders to help operationalize them and demonstrate how they can contribute to the fight. That challenge becomes particularly important as the service develops capabilities such as Collaborative Combat Aircraft. Niemi pointed to the cultural shift required to embrace technology that could eventually perform tasks traditionally handled by pilots. “I can imagine a day in the future, 10 years, maybe more, where a CCA autonomous algorithm does a better job flying a fighter airplane than I did as a captain,” Niemi said. “That hurts my ego a little bit, but at the same time, I see that this trend is happening.” The panel closed with a discussion on whether the Air Force should continue refining existing concepts or develop entirely new ones. Spain pointed that to find the answer, start by asking what problem the service is actually trying to solve. Then look at if the current CONOP that exists sufficiently addresses the problem or could it if it was modified. If it cannot, he said, you probably need to transition to a concept that will. “This stuff is really hard, and a lot of smart people have tried to do this the best they could under the conditions within they were working and now it is our turn,” Spain said. “We are committed to … making the best decisions that we can for the Air Force today, while also preparing our Air Force for the Future.” Ultimately, the panelists emphasized that building the future Air Force will require more than new platforms. It will require resilient Airmen, infrastructure and logistics, risk-informed decision-making and a willingness to put emerging capabilities into the hands of warfighters to determine what works. As the service prepares for an increasingly contested fight, the panel underscored the need to remain ready for today's fight while continually shaping the force needed for what comes next.

items.title: Long-range penetrating force remains at forefront of bomber operations
items.author: Justin Oakes
items.summary: Panelists emphasized that sustaining deterrence requires continuous bomber fleet modernization, resilient communications, low-observable technologies, and strong industrial base partnerships.
items.body:
Published Sept. 16, 2026

By Justin Oakes

Eighth Air Force and Joint-Global Strike Operations Center Public Affairs

Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury — or at least the lessons learned — were the topics of discussion at a long-range airpower panel during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Sept. 15.

The panel brought together bomber, mobility, and aerospace industry leaders to assess the strategic airpower environment.

Throughout the dialogue, panel members emphasized that while long-range strike operations have proven decisively effective in recent combat campaigns, maintaining that asymmetric advantage demands continuous modernization, seamless cross-command teamwork, and a strong partnership with the defense industrial base.

Maj. Gen. Ty Neuman , Eighth Air Force and Joint-Global Strike Operations Center commander, began by highlighting the inherent stamina of the nation's bomber fleet. “We are a ready force that demonstrated our endurance,” Neuman said, emphasizing how Eighth Air Force ’s constant readiness provides tailored deterrence and reassurance across the globe.

Reflecting on the sheer logistical and operational coordination demanded during Operation Epic Fury, Neuman praised the joint commitment across the enterprise, noting that “everyone has been all in.” He stressed that the unmatched long-range strike capability demonstrated in both Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury delivers an unmistakable message to adversaries: no one should question the readiness or capability of the United States to hold targets at risk anytime, anywhere.

Panelists later discussed the necessity of denying adversaries safe havens and operational sanctuaries, where Neuman outlined why standoff weapons alone cannot shoulder the strategic burden. Potential adversaries continue to harden facilities, bury critical infrastructure, and construct heavily defended anti-access perimeters.

“Not every target can be hit by long-range standoff weapons; we need a penetrating force,” the Eighth Air Force commander said. “Modernizing the legacy bomber fleet is an imperative to denying sanctuary to our adversaries.”

To outpace emerging threats, the Air Force is advancing a complementary mix of weapons and platforms, including standoff systems and stand-in penetrating capabilities. Ongoing modernization efforts include expanding the B-1’s beyond-line-of-sight communication systems, outfitting the B-2 Spirit with advanced radar enhancement programs to bolster survivability in anti-access environments, and exploring expanded payloads for the B-2 fleet.

When operating against advanced air defense systems, stealth remains paramount. “All-aspect low observable weapon systems are a non-negotiable price to entry,” Neuman underscored.

The conversation then moved to the future viability of stealth in an era of proliferating air defense systems.

Neuman affirmed that low observability is not a passing technological phase, but a foundational requirement for the future fight.

He emphasized that the Air Force must pursue both low-observable aircraft and low-observable complementary munitions to survive and deliver effects inside contested airspace. Echoing this assessment, the panel moderator noted that stealth is fundamentally about disrupting the enemy’s integrated kill chain, denying adversaries the ability to detect, track, and engage U.S. strike platforms before mission completion.

The evolving nature of the battlespace, where multi-domain environments are saturated with unmanned systems, electromagnetic interference, and missile salvos, was another topic of discussion.

Industry panelist Jamie Burgess of Boeing cautioned that sheer data volume does not automatically equate to combat capability.

“One can drown in data and starve for information,” Burgess remarked, pointing out the necessity of delivering processed, actionable intelligence directly to aircrews and operational commanders.

The panel discussed how the battle network and integrated command, control, and communications architectures must synthesize real-time data from space, cyber, and airborne assets into coherent situational awareness that accelerates combat decision-making.

Diving into fleet viability and continuous modernization, the general highlighted the operational strain and lessons realized from long-duration strike missions. During Operation Epic Fury, bomber sorties averaged 38 hours in duration — demanding extraordinary human stamina, aircraft reliability, and extensive air refueling support.

According to the Air Mobility Command panelist, “it took dozens and dozens of tankers to execute Operation Epic Fury,” illustrating the indispensable synergy between Air Force Global Strike Command and AMC.

When looking at the service’s age of the inventory, Neuman noted that “our youngest bomber is 30-plus years old.” While airframes have proven durable, sustained investment in modern digital avionics, resilient beyond-line-of-sight connectivity, and modern propulsion is essential across every platform.

The bomber force commander called for a fundamental pivot in weapons integration philosophy: rather than undertaking costly and complex modifications to alter legacy aircraft around new weapons, future munitions must be intentionally designed to seamlessly integrate into existing bomber bays and pylons.

“Bombers must deliver strategic options to the president,” Neuman emphasized, noting that modernization ensures the commander in chief retains flexible, credible conventional and nuclear response options.

Examining the role of industry innovation, Neuman praised the ingenuity of maintenance and logistics Airmen who keep vintage platforms flight-ready, but stressed that the service cannot accomplish sustainment alone.

“It is about partnerships, clear and concise requirements, and giving industry the ability to run with it. It’s a team effort,” Neuman remarked, underscoring the urgent requirement to bolster the defense industrial base and maintain reliable supply chains for critical components.

The panel then concluded by addressing Total Force Integration.

“This is a Total Force Integration effort for every single component,” Neuman said.

“Allies and partners, we have your back. We are the free world’s only long-range strike capability, and we will continue to deliver anytime, anywhere.”

items.title: Legal and Clinical Liability of Comanaging Pediatric Mental Health With Unregulated AI Chatbots
items.author: Hao Yu
items.summary: We conclude that parents and clinicians should proactively discuss chatbot use to promote safety, appropriate expectations, and linkages to evidence-based care.
items.body:
ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026Published in: JAMA Pediatrics (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.3929

In Reply: We thank Lennon for highlighting an issue that requires serious legal and policy attention as adolescents increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health advice. However, we believe the letter rests on a premise that mischaracterizes the conclusions of our article.1 We did not recommend clinicians comanage, police, or actively integrate unregulated chatbots into pediatric mental health care. Rather, we reported that nearly 1 in 5 US adolescents and young adults had used AI chatbots for mental health advice, that most users found them helpful, and that 63.3% disclosed this use to no one. On that basis, we concluded that parents and clinicians should proactively discuss chatbot use to promote safety, appropriate expectations, and linkages to evidence-based care.

items.title: Army Chaplains’ Perceptions About Identifying, Intervening, and Referring Soldiers at Risk of Suicide
items.author: Aaron Kofner
items.summary: In this study, we estimate perceptions of Army chaplains and CAs in domains relevant to gatekeeping, including intervention efficacy, reluctance to intervene, stigma, and past intervention behavior.
items.body: In U.S. Army policy, chaplains and chaplain assistants (CAs) are explicitly identified as primary gatekeepers; however, research on their perceptions about their roles identifying, caring for, and referring soldiers in suicidal distress is scant. In this study, we estimate perceptions of Army chaplains and CAs in domains relevant to gatekeeping, including intervention efficacy, reluctance to intervene, stigma, and past intervention behavior. We do so using an online survey that was administered to all chaplains and CAs in the Army’s Active Component and Reserves in 2012. Response rates ranged from 41% of all chaplains in the Active Component to 19% of chaplains and CAs in the Reserves. Almost half of all chaplains and CAs thought they could use more suicide prevention training. Although chaplains reported greater perceived ability to intervene with individuals at risk for suicide relative to civilian samples, they also reported more reluctance to intervene. This reluctance may be explained in part by high reports of stigma regarding mental health treatment. These findings suggest that the Army should implement specific suicide prevention training for chaplains and CAs that focuses on providing acute behavioral health treatment, reducing mental health stigma, and encouraging chaplains to collaborate with other behavioral health resources.

items.title: Evolving Health and Wellbeing of Thalidomide Survivors as They Age
items.author: Agne Ulyte
items.summary: This scoping review updates the 2017 review by exploring evidence published 2017-2025 on the physical, mental, and social wellbeing of ageing thalidomide survivors, identifying emerging health issues, care needs, and evidence gaps.
items.body:
A Scoping Review Update (2017-2025)

ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026Published in: Disabilities, Volume 6, Issue 4 (August 2026). DOI: 10.3390/disabilities6040067

Thalidomide, prescribed to pregnant women in the late 1950s and early 1960s, caused severe congenital impairments known as thalidomide embryopathy, yet the long-term health and wellbeing of survivors as they reach older adulthood remains underexplored.

This scoping review updates the 2017 Newbronner and Atkin review by exploring evidence published between 2017 and 2025 on the physical, mental, and social wellbeing of ageing thalidomide survivors, identifying emerging health issues, care needs, and evidence gaps.

Searches across nine academic databases and grey literature sources identified studies reporting health, wellbeing, or quality of life among middle-aged and older adults with documented prenatal thalidomide exposure.

Thirty papers from the UK, Germany, Japan, Italy, Sweden, Canada, and Australia were included, showing pervasive musculoskeletal deterioration, chronic pain, and increased metabolic disorders. Mental health conditions, including depression, anxiety, and stress, were common and often linked to pain severity and functional limitations, alongside sensory impairments, dental issues, and functional decline, though many survivors demonstrated resilience.

Ageing thalidomide survivors face complex, progressive health challenges that extend beyond congenital impairments, highlighting a need for coordinated, specialist care to support wellbeing in later life.

items.title: Do Stigma and Efficacy Mediate the Association Between Training and Suicide Prevention Behavior Among Army Noncommissioned Officers?
items.author: Lisa Wagner
items.summary: We surveyed Army NCOs to determine if training on suicide prevention and soft skills was associated with gatekeeper behavior and use of soft skills, and whether that association was explained by stigma and perceptions of efficacy.
items.body:
Rates of suicide in the Active Component of the military have significantly increased since 2010, with particularly high rates among Army service members. One element of the Army's approach to suicide prevention relies on noncommissioned officers (NCOs) as gatekeepers who have regular contact with soldiers. NCOs receive suicide prevention training, but there is limited evidence that such training leads to behavior change.

We surveyed 2468 Army NCOs participating in leadership development courses to determine (a) if training on suicide prevention and soft skills (e.g., active listening) was associated with gatekeeper behavior and use of soft skills; and (b) whether that association was explained by two potential barriers, stigma and perceptions of efficacy.

Both the number of suicide prevention training topics and soft skills trained were associated with increased gatekeeper behavior; these relationships were explained in part by lower stigma and higher efficacy for use of soft skills. The use of interactive training methods and receiving coaching after training were not associated with stigma or efficacy, though both methods were associated with more frequent use of soft skills.

Results suggest that the content and format of training is important to preparing NCOs to fulfill a gatekeeper role.

items.title: Preventing the Creation of Mirror Life
items.author: Krista Langeland
items.summary: This brief summarizes RAND research on steps the United States could take to prevent the creation of mirror life—a synthetic life form that could pose irreversible risks—before the window for meaningful action closes.
items.body:
A Strategy for the United States

Research SummaryPublished Sep 16, 2026

The creation of mirror life—a hypothetical life form, such as a bacterium, built from biomolecules with the opposite molecular structure of all known life on earth—could cause fatal infections in multicellular life, including humans, animals, and plants, and upend entire ecosystems. In July 2026, RAND published A U.S. Strategy to Prevent the Creation of Mirror Life, which overviews two lines of effort (LOEs) that U.S. policymakers could pursue to prevent mirror life from becoming reality. This brief summarizes these LOEs, the policy levers called for by each LOE, and the principles and analysis on which they are built.

Mirror life is a hypothetical form of life built from biomolecules with the opposite molecular structure of all known life on earth. Although mirror life does not yet exist, experts estimate that creation of the first mirror bacterium—a likely first instantiation of mirror life—could be technically feasible within the next few decades and could potentially cost as little as several hundred million dollars.

Mirror life’s reverse molecular structure could enable mirror bacteria to (1) escape immune detection and cause fatal infections, (2) avoid natural predators, and (3) proliferate throughout natural ecosystems. If created and released, whether accidentally or intentionally, mirror bacteria could potentially spread widely, causing irreversible harm.

The policy challenge that mirror life presents is both urgent and unusual. Scientists have produced mirror-image biomolecules that could serve as the building blocks of mirror life. Much of the research that moves science closer to realizing mirror bacteria is not inherently dangerous, has demonstrated benefits or promises benefits, and is likely to continue for reasons unrelated to the creation of mirror life. However, mirror life itself is expected to have few plausible benefits. Despite this, some actors might still wish to pursue mirror life, such as well-intentioned researchers who overlook the risks associated with mirror life or malicious actors who seek to acquire or use mirror life as a doomsday capability.

Traditional governance approaches for emerging technologies—such as post-hoc regulation or adaptive oversight—rely on the opportunity to mitigate risks as they emerge and before they become crises. These approaches might be ill-suited to govern mirror life. This is because once a single viable mirror bacterium exists, the knowledge and methods for making riskier variants could proliferate rapidly, and even seemingly benign strains of such bacteria could be modified to be more dangerous. The first successful creation of mirror life could therefore represent an irreversible threshold: a point after which containment and control become far more difficult and perhaps even impossible.

Only a small number of scientifically advanced actors possess the capacity to pursue mirror life. For the foreseeable future, less advanced actors—including isolated or sanctioned regimes, nonstate groups, and individuals—lack the infrastructure, expertise, and access to materials that are required to create mirror life without assistance from the global scientific community. This asymmetry has an important strategic implication: Should the few scientific powers capable of creating mirror life agree on the need to prevent it, their restraint effectively denies the means of creating it to all others.

The United States, as one of the world’s leading scientific powers and a global hub for bioscience and biotechnology, is uniquely positioned to influence the global trajectory of mirror life development and therefore should lead international efforts to prevent its creation. U.S. actions can help establish international restraint, although preventing mirror life ultimately depends on sustained cooperation among the major scientific powers—particularly China—because no country can manage the risk alone.

RAND researchers guided U.S. policymakers in developing a strategy to address the risks posed by mirror life before scientific progress or geopolitical incentives close the window for meaningful action. Rather than predicting whether mirror life will pose catastrophic risk with certainty, the authors treat the expert assessment that mirror life could pose unacceptable risks as sufficient motivation for strategic planning now.

RAND researchers identified the following four principles, which guide the development of a strategy:

- Prevention over mitigation: Because the first mirror bacterium could trigger irreversible consequences and enable the rapid proliferation of mirror life capabilities, governance, norms, and constraints must be established before mirror life exists—rather than governments and other actors relying on mitigation after the fact.

- Universal restraint over partial restraint: Even a single actor creating mirror life could pose a global risk. Prevention depends on broadly shared restraint supported by coordinated governance, transparency, and scientific norms.

- Transparency over secrecy: A shared understanding of mirror life’s risks and confidence that others are exercising restraint are essential for preventing competitive dynamics and sustaining collective prevention efforts.

- Cooperation over coercion: Because no country can eliminate the risk alone, prevention requires trusted international cooperation that preserves legitimacy and encourages broad participation rather than coercive measures.

RAND researchers identified policy levers that policymakers could consider, specifically those that (1) reduce incentives to develop mirror life and (2) detect and deter early-stage development of mirror life. Other levers—such as those that disrupt or punish advanced development or build countermeasures and resilience—are inconsistent with the four strategic principles and therefore do not factor into a U.S. preventive strategy.

The U.S. strategy organizes levers into the following LOEs (Figure 1):

- LOE 1—Engage scientific superpowers, especially China, to build the foundation for collective restraint. This LOE prioritizes transparent scientific collaboration, shared risk assessments, and early norm-setting to discourage major powers from viewing mirror life as a strategic advantage and to prevent mirror life research from becoming an arena for geopolitical competition. LOE 1 shapes the incentives for major scientific powers and academic institutions and has a cascading impact on other nation-states and commercial firms. Although LOE 1’s direct influence on other actors is more limited, broadly stigmatizing mirror life could still create reputational and operational barriers for malign actors.

- LOE 2—Establish collective restraint across domestic, allied, and competing scientific communities. This LOE combines measures that reduce the incentives and increase the costs of creating mirror life. Together, these actions shift motivations and capabilities away from mirror life development for states, commercial firms, research institutions, and multilateral bodies.

In pursuing these LOEs, the United States should:

- Commit clearly to not developing mirror life, even if other actors are suspected of pursuing it. This commitment reflects the fact that the possession of mirror life would not provide protection, deterrence, or resilience against mirror life developed by others and would instead exacerbate global risk.

- Take great caution with actions or statements that could foster mistrust or spur strategic competition in the field of mirror life or its enabling technologies, particularly actions or statements that are related to disrupting mirror life development or investing in countermeasures and resilience.

- Advance actions with longer lead times as soon as possible. Legislation, international engagement, technology development for detection and verification, and treaty-creation groundwork require years to mature. These efforts should begin now and evolve as new information emerges.

- Exclude coercive measures from the strategy at this time. Actions that rely on pressure, disruption, or punishment would erode trust and cooperation among major scientific powers on which prevention depends. Such measures should be out of scope at this time. If such measures ever become appropriate, they should be pursued cooperatively and transparently, not unilaterally.

- Treat countermeasures and resilience as later-resort measures. These measures are unlikely to be effective against the proliferation of mirror life and the ensuing risks. Premature or unilateral investment in defensive preparations could inadvertently weaken deterrence, advance the science of mirror life, and trigger counterproductive dynamics.

By strengthening trust, transparency, and cooperative incentives, the United States can help ensure that those with the means to develop mirror life choose not to—and, in doing so, make mirror life’s pursuit infeasible for everyone else.

items.title: The Insurability of Artificial Intelligence
items.author: Celine Robinson
items.summary: A mismatch exists between rapid enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the market for insuring it. This report examines AI incidents, lawsuits, laws, and insurance filings to assess coverage responses and accumulation risks.
items.body:
ResearchPublished Sep 16, 2026

A mismatch exists between rapid enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the fragmented market for insuring AI-related losses. This report examines AI incidents, U.S. lawsuits, enacted state laws, and insurance filings to assess how insurers are responding through exclusions, endorsements, affirmative coverage, or silence.

Businesses increasingly embed artificial intelligence (AI) in operations, products, and services, creating both new opportunities and new forms of risk. Firms are deploying AI in customer service, employment screening, coding, fraud detection, and autonomous systems. At the same time, AI-related harms are already emerging, including incorrect or misleading outputs, deepfakes, privacy violations, intellectual property disputes, fraud, product defects, and discriminatory decisions. These harms create demand for insurance but do not fit neatly within existing insurance lines.

In this report, the authors examine AI incidents, U.S. lawsuits, enacted state laws, and admitted-market insurance filings to assess how insurers are responding through exclusions, endorsements, affirmative coverage, or silence. Key findings include the dominance of misinformation incidents, concentration of litigation around intellectual property, and five mechanisms through which AI could generate accumulation losses across insurance lines.

- Of public generative AI incidents, 84 percent relate to misinformation (false, deceptive, or manipulative content) and deepfakes (AI-generated or altered media impersonating a real person or event).

- Of U.S. litigation for generative AI harms, 60 percent relate to the alleged violations of intellectual property or improper training by AI developers rather than to the use, misuse, or outputs of these models.

- Most U.S. states have adopted laws focusing on restricting harmful synthetic content, such as nonconsensual intimate images and child sexual abuse material.

- Unlike cyber, AI risks are not contained to a single insurance line but span many lines: technology errors and omissions and professional liability, cyber, directors and officers, commercial property, and more.

- Insurance carriers are responding to AI risks unevenly, with some offering affirmative coverage for certain risks (e.g., model errors), and others filing broad exclusions for any AI-related loss.

- Most carriers are remaining silent, neither affirming nor excluding AI-related risks in their policies, leaving coverage for such losses untested and open to dispute.

- State insurance regulators and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, supported by carriers and brokers, should develop an AI Coverage Notice enabling carriers to clarify how, and under which lines, AI-related losses are affirmatively covered, excluded, or left silent.

- Incident reporting for attritional and accumulation loss should be standardized. Policy researchers and brokers, together with carriers and reinsurers, should develop a common, adaptable taxonomy for AI incidents, claims, and controls to properly track and report on AI risks. Actual incident data should remain private, however.

- Insurers and reinsurers should analyze AI aggregation scenarios, focusing on shared model dependency, common infrastructure failure, and regulatory shock to manage correlated AI risk.

items.author: Arthur T. DeGaetano
items.summary: This climate summary aims to inform Mid-Atlantic policymakers and practitioners about weather patterns during the 2026 summer season, regional climate trends, and the upcoming fall season.
items.body:
ToolPublished Sep 16, 2026

The Mid-Atlantic Regional Climate Impacts Summary and Outlook is a quarterly series produced by the Mid-Atlantic Regional Integrated Science and Assessments (MARISA) program, a collaboration funded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration through the RAND Corporation and researchers at Pennsylvania State University, Carnegie Mellon University, Johns Hopkins University, Morgan State University, Cornell University, and the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. This series draws information from regional climate centers, news and weather information, and high-resolution climate data sets for the benefit of policymakers, practitioners, residents, and community leaders in the Mid-Atlantic region, with a focus on the Chesapeake Bay watershed. Projections of future climate in the Mid-Atlantic region come from the best available scientific information. For this summer 2026 version of the series, Part 1 details significant weather events that occurred from June through August 2026; Part 2 characterizes seasonal temperature and precipitation compared to historical averages; Part 3 describes seasonal weather forecasts and pertinent information for the upcoming fall season; and Part four provides a primer on the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), how it will impact weather in the Mid-Atlantic and how it is projected to change in the future.

items.title: Positioning Qatar in the Global Research, Development, and Innovation Landscape
items.author: Sara Zikri
items.summary: Qatar aims to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem. This report benchmarks Qatar against other small advanced economies and identifies policy options to close gaps in STEM talent, research, and innovation capacity.
items.body:
Comparative Insights from Small Advanced Economies

ResearchPublished Sep 16, 2026

Qatar aims to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem. This report benchmarks Qatar against other small advanced economies, examines international policy practices, and evaluates its national strategies. It identifies weak STEM interest, fragmented researcher support, retention challenges linked to short visas, and limited industry–academia collaboration, and sets out policy options to address these gaps.

Qatar has articulated a bold vision to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem, as set out in the Third National Development Strategy and the Qatar Research Development and Innovation Council's 2030 Strategy. These strategies set ambitious targets for expanding the RDI talent pool, raising government investment in research and innovation, and improving outputs such as high-impact publications, patents and start-ups.

This report assesses the current state of Qatar's RDI ecosystem by benchmarking performance indicators against other small, advanced economies, examining international policy practices, and evaluating the effects of Qatar's national strategies on research and innovation outcomes. It highlights areas of relative strength and identifies policy options to address persistent gaps.

The most significant challenge identified is the relatively low level of interest and attainment in STEM disciplines among Qatari students, which weakens the domestic talent pipeline. Although national strategies recognise the importance of STEM education, a comprehensive and coordinated action plan is lacking. Support for early-career researchers is also fragmented, and retention of skilled international talent is constrained by short visa durations and limited employment flexibility. Collaboration between research institutions and the private sector remains limited, restricting the translation of knowledge into innovation.

The study finds that the Qatar National Vision 2030 has positively influenced research and innovation outputs, even amid regional and global disruptions, and the more recent QRDI 2030 Strategy shows early signs of effectiveness, though it is too soon to assess its full impact. Future evaluations should incorporate broader indicators and longitudinal data.

Linkages between research institutions and the private sector remain weak, constraining the translation of knowledge into innovation. While the business set-up process is relatively streamlined, set-up costs have been high relative to comparator economies, standing at 6.3% of GNI per capita in 2019, though recent developments suggest significant reductions. Against a backdrop of declining total factor productivity, revitalising the private sector through entrepreneurship and innovation is increasingly important. Existing infrastructure such as QSTP and Education City offers a foundation on which closer co-location and coordination between academia and industry can be built.

Support for early-career researchers is fragmented and administered largely by individual universities, producing variable training quality. Recent visa reforms, including the Mustaqel visa and the abandonment of the Kafala system, have improved conditions for migrant researchers, but short visa durations and limited employment flexibility continue to push international talent away, often before researchers can secure subsequent employment.

The relatively low level of interest and attainment in STEM disciplines among Qatari students weakens the domestic talent pipeline and limits capacity to meet future workforce demands. Despite improvements in attainment over the past decade, Qatar continues to underperform in science and mathematics relative to other small, advanced economies. National strategies acknowledge STEM's importance, but no concrete, coordinated action plan is in place.

- Qatar may wish to consider a coordinated STEM action plan spanning early to adult education, with clearer roles and stronger teacher development. Finland and New Zealand's teacher-led communities of practice offer useful reference points.

- There may be value in exploring a nationally administered fellowship scheme for early-career researchers, drawing on Singapore's approach, alongside greater visa flexibility informed by models such as Ireland's.

- Building on QSTP and Education City, Qatar could consider cluster-based approaches, with QRDI well placed to help coordinate and evaluate support.
